main.claim: Upload a photo or screenshot up to 15 MB and the tool returns the text in it, in reading order, within a few seconds. Copy it with one click. Free: 3 runs a day, 3 more after you leave an email, and no account needed.

sections.heading: How to turn an image into text
sections.body:
Open the tool in any browser on your phone or computer. Pick the image you want to read. It can be a photo of a sign, a printed page or a receipt, or a screenshot of text on your screen.

1. Open [Image to Text](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/).
2. Choose the image file from your device.
3. Wait a few seconds for the text to come back.
4. Click copy, then paste the text where you need it.

**The result is plain text.** You get the words only, in the order they appear in the picture, with line breaks kept. The tool does not add a summary, a description of the picture or a translation.

sections.heading: What the result looks like
sections.body:
The tool reads the text in reading order and keeps each line on its own line. It does not keep bold, italics, font sizes or the layout of the page, so a table or a set of columns may come back as plain lines of text. If the picture has no text at all, the tool replies with the words No text found.

Read the result against the picture before you use it. Small print, blur, glare and curved pages cause most of the mistakes. If a word looks wrong, go back to the picture, fix that word, and move on.

sections.heading: Free runs and limits
sections.body:
The free plan gives you 3 runs a day. Leave an email address and you get 3 more. You do not need an account to start, and there is no app to install. Files can be up to 15 MB. For an image, the answer usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds.

If your file is too large, crop the picture to the text you need and try again.

sections.heading: What happens to your image
sections.body:
The tool runs on Lazur's servers. Your image is sent there, and Google Gemini reads the text in it. Do not upload a picture with private details you would not send to a server, such as a bank card, a passport or a medical form.

For the best result, use a sharp photo with even light, or a full-size screenshot of the text. Hold the phone straight above the page so the lines are not curved.

sections.heading: Read text on your phone or Mac too
sections.body:
Each platform has a built-in route as well. On iPhone, Live Text copies text straight from a photo, and the steps are on the [iPhone page](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/iphone). On a Mac, you can select text in Preview, and the steps are on the [Mac page](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/mac). If you need the text in a document, the [Word page](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/word) shows the fastest way to paste it.

If you type up what is on your screen every day, Lazur is a Mac app for that. Hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

sections.heading: How AI reads text in an image

sections.heading: What the AI returns, and what it does not
sections.body:
The reply is the text as it is written on the picture. Here is what you can expect:

- The words as written, including any spelling mistakes that are printed on the page.
- No summary, no description of the picture and no translation.
- Plain text only. Bold, italics and layout are not kept.
- If the picture has no text, the reply is: No text found.

The AI can still misread a word. Check the result against the picture, most of all for numbers, names and codes.

sections.heading: Pick the right picture
sections.body: Use a photo or screenshot where the text fills most of the frame. Printed pages, signs, labels, slides and screenshots of articles all give clean results. Text on a busy background, lines that run at an angle, and text that is cut off at the edge of the picture are the most likely to come back with mistakes. If you can, retake the photo with the page flat and the light even, or crop the picture closer to the words.

sections.heading: When the AI gets it wrong
sections.body:
Blur, glare, low light and tiny text cause most errors. Take the picture again with the page flat and the light even, then run it again. Check numbers, names, dates and codes first, because a single wrong digit changes the meaning.

If you need an exact copy of a document for legal or medical use, compare the full result with the original line by line before you rely on it. Read the whole reply once against the picture before you paste it into another document.

A clear photo of a single page is easier to read than a long, multi-page shot. If your text runs over two pages, take two pictures, run them one after the other, then join the results in order.

sections.heading: Copy the text from an image into Word
sections.body:
Word does not copy the words out of a picture you insert. The picture stays a picture. To get editable text, read the image first, then paste the words into your document.

1. Open the [image to text tool for Word](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/word).
2. Choose the photo or screenshot, up to 15 MB.
3. Wait for the text to come back.
4. Click copy, switch to Word, click where the text should go, and press Ctrl+V on Windows or Command+V on a Mac.

sections.heading: What you get in Word
sections.body: The tool returns plain text, so headings, bold, italics, columns and tables from the picture are not kept. Line breaks are kept, so each line of the image starts a new line in Word. Set your own formatting after you paste. That takes less time than retyping the words, and you control how the document looks.

sections.heading: Copy text from a picture in OneNote
sections.body:
Microsoft's text-from-picture feature sits in OneNote, not in Word. In the OneNote desktop app, the steps are in [Microsoft's OCR guide](https://support.microsoft.com/office/93a70a2f-ebcd-42dc-9f0b-19b09fd775b4).

1. Right-click the picture in OneNote.
2. Select Copy Text from Picture.
3. Click where you want the text, then press Ctrl+V.

If you do not see Copy Text from Picture, the text may still be processing. Microsoft says complex or hard-to-read images can take longer, possibly a day or two, so wait a few moments and try again. You can paste the text from OneNote into Word the same way.

sections.heading: Check the text before you use it
sections.body: OCR accuracy depends on the quality of the image, and Microsoft advises you to proofread the result. Columns and tables often come out poorly, so check those parts most carefully. If a picture is at an angle, straighten it or retake it before you copy, because a tilted line can merge with the line above it. Fix the words in Word, not in the picture. If the table or columns matter, copy the text in small blocks, one section at a time, and rebuild the table in Word by hand. That keeps each block readable and makes the mistakes easier to spot.

sections.heading: Limits and privacy
sections.body: Free use is 3 runs a day, with 3 more after you leave an email. Files can be up to 15 MB. The image is sent to Lazur's servers, where Google Gemini reads the text, so keep private documents out of the upload. Each picture counts as one run, so a long document with many pages uses up your free runs quickly. Read the page you need first, and send only that picture.

faq.q: How do I convert an image to text in Word?
faq.a: Inserting the picture does not copy its text. Upload the image to this tool, click copy, then press Ctrl+V in Word. In the OneNote desktop app, you can right-click a picture and choose Copy Text from Picture instead, then paste into Word.

Microsoft's OCR feature is in OneNote, not in Word itself. In the OneNote desktop app, right-click a picture and choose Copy Text from Picture, then paste the result into Word. This tool gives you the text without opening OneNote.

faq.q: Can I edit the text after I convert it?
faq.a: Yes. Paste it into Word and edit as normal. The tool returns plain text, so you will need to add headings and bold again. Proofread the result, because small text and columns can come out wrong.

pages.description: Copy the text from a photo on iPhone with Live Text, or use this free tool in Safari. Step by step, 3 free runs a day, no app needed.
pages.claim: Your iPhone can copy text from a photo with Live Text: open the photo, press and hold a word, and tap Copy. In Safari, this free image to text tool also works, with a plain text result you copy in one click. No app.

sections.heading: Copy text from a photo with Live Text
sections.body:
Live Text is built into iOS, so there is nothing to install. It needs an iPhone XS, iPhone XR or later with iOS 15 or later. [Apple's guide](https://support.apple.com/en-us/120004) has the official steps.

1. Open the Photos app and choose the photo.
2. Press and hold a word, then drag the grab points to set the selection.
3. Tap Copy. To grab all the text, tap Select All.
4. Paste the text into another app, or share it.

Apple also shows a Live Text button in the lower-right corner of a photo. Tap it to highlight all the text in the picture.

sections.heading: If Live Text is not working
sections.body: Open Settings, tap General, then Language & Region, and turn on Live Text. Live Text for video needs iOS 16 or later. On iPad, Live Text needs iPadOS 15.1 or later.

sections.heading: Use the tool in Safari
sections.body:
If the text is in a screenshot you saved, a file you downloaded or a picture from another app, use this tool in Safari instead. Open the [iPhone image to text page](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/iphone), choose the image file, wait a few seconds, and tap copy. The result is plain text, with line breaks kept. Open the photo or file you want to read first, so you know the picture is the right one before you use one of your free runs for the day.

The tool is free to use: 3 runs a day, with 3 more after you leave an email. Files can be up to 15 MB.

sections.heading: Check the result
sections.body: Live Text and the tool both make mistakes on small, blurry or curved text. Look at the copied words next to the photo, and fix any word that does not match before you use it. Numbers, dates and codes deserve the closest look, because one wrong character changes what the text says. A photo taken with the phone held straight above the page usually gives the cleanest copy. If the first copy has gaps, take a closer photo of the missing part and copy that part separately, then put the two pieces together in the order they appear on the page.

sections.heading: Privacy and sending the image
sections.body: Live Text is Apple's built-in feature. The Safari tool is different: it sends the image to Lazur's servers, where Google Gemini reads the text. Keep private documents, card numbers and IDs out of that upload, and use Live Text for those photos instead. A photo of a form with personal details is a good example of a picture to copy in Photos rather than upload.

faq.q: How do I turn an image into text on iPhone?
faq.a: Open the photo in the Photos app, press and hold a word, drag the grab points to select the text you want, and tap Copy. Use Select All to copy everything in the picture. This needs Live Text, which works on iPhone XS, iPhone XR or later with iOS 15 or later.

faq.q: Why can't I copy text from an image on my iPhone?
faq.a: Check that your iPhone supports Live Text, which needs iPhone XS, iPhone XR or later with iOS 15 or later. Then open Settings, tap General, then Language & Region, and turn on Live Text. If it is still off, use the image to text tool in Safari instead.
Yes. Apple calls it Live Text. It finds text in photos, and you can copy, paste or share what it finds. For text that is not in Photos, or on an older iPhone, a web tool in Safari is another option.

sections.heading: Copy text from an image in Preview
sections.body:
Preview can copy text from a photo or from a screenshot saved as an image file. [Apple's Preview guide](https://support.apple.com/guide/preview/prvw625a5b2c/mac) covers the steps.

1. Open the image in Preview.
2. Hold the pointer over the text, then drag to select the words you want.
3. Control-click the selection and choose Copy Text.
4. Paste the text into another document or app.

Preview is the right choice when the image is already open on your Mac and you want a few lines. You copy only what you select, so you control the exact words that go into your document.

sections.heading: If you cannot select the text
sections.body: Choose Tools, then Text Selection from the menu bar to turn on the Text Selection tool. Then drag across the words again. Once the tool is on, the text in the image becomes selectable, and you can copy it the same way. If the text still does not select, check that the image is a clear file rather than a picture that is too small or too dark, then open it again.

sections.heading: Use the tool in your browser
sections.body:
If you have a photo or screenshot and want the whole text at once, skip Preview. Open the [Mac image to text page](https://image-to-text.lazur.app/mac) in your browser, choose the file, and copy the result. Files can be up to 15 MB. The result is plain text, so you may need to add headings and bold text again afterward.

The tool is free to use: 3 runs a day, with 3 more after you leave an email. You do not need an account or an app.

sections.heading: Take a screenshot first
sections.body: The tools read images, so text on your screen needs a screenshot first. Take the screenshot, save it as an image file, then open it in Preview or upload it to the tool. The copied text is only as clean as the picture, so take the screenshot at full size and keep the text sharp. If the window is small, enlarge it before you take the screenshot, so the letters are large enough to read.

sections.heading: Check the result and your privacy
sections.body: Small text, glare and curved pages cause most errors. Check the copied words against the image before you use them. The browser tool sends the image to Lazur's servers, where Google Gemini reads it. Keep private documents out of that upload, and use Preview for anything you do not want to send. A long document is easier to handle one page at a time, so select and copy in Preview page by page, and paste each part into the same document in order.

faq.q: How do I copy text from a picture on Mac?
faq.a: Open the picture in Preview, hold the pointer over the text, and drag to select it. Control-click the selection and choose Copy Text. Then paste it into any app. If you cannot select the text, choose Tools, then Text Selection in the menu bar.

faq.q: Does Apple have built-in OCR on Mac?
faq.a: Yes. Apple calls the feature Live Text. It finds text in images in apps such as Preview, so you can select and copy the words. For a plain text result in any browser, this free tool takes files up to 15 MB.

faq.q: Can I convert an image to text on a Mac for free?
faq.a: Yes. Preview's Copy Text feature costs nothing. The browser tool here gives 3 free runs a day, and 3 more after you leave an email address. No account and no app are needed for the browser tool.
